extraction_notes.note: Stated in theorem environments titled 'Axiom: ...' and postulated without proof; typed assumption rather than theorem.
Most results are described in words with the actual statements living in Lean code; the theorems oneOpLHS_equiv/oneOpRHS_equiv have no mathematical content in the text.

Overview chapter, code listings, engineering prose (code structure, compilation time, gas sorries, future work) and a reference to an X-function theorem whose statement is absent from the source were not extracted.
The project's overarching bisimulation goal: open_problem rather than problem, since it is an unresolved statement to prove, not a computational task.

nodes.name: hooked function (hook attribute)
nodes.statement: K productions can have a \texttt{hook} attribute (e.g., \href{https://github.com/runtimeverification/k/blob/master/k-distribution/include/kframework/builtin/domains.md#integer-and-bytes-conversion}{converting integers to bytes}), which tells K that the production will rely on an implementation from the target backend with a given name.
also_stated_at: Some functions in K are left for the backends to implement. These are called ``hooked functions''.
nodes.statement_short: A K production with a hook attribute relies on an implementation supplied by the target backend.

nodes.name: Rewrites type
nodes.statement: Rules extracted to Lean from K will be enconded as constructors of this type. We have that \texttt{Rewrites : SortGeneratedTopCell → SortGeneratedTopCell → Prop} where \href{https://runtimeverification.github.io/evm-equivalence/docs/EvmEquivalence/KEVM2Lean/Sorts.html#SortGeneratedTopCell}{\texttt{SortGeneratedTopCell}} is the type for KEVM states. Given \texttt{p}, \texttt{p'} : \texttt{SortGeneratedTopCell}, \texttt{Rewrites p p'} means that the KEVM state \texttt{p} rewrites to \texttt{p'}. All of the \texttt{requires} clauses of a rule are encoded as the corresponding constructor's arguments. There's an special transitivy rule that ensures the chaining of multiple rewrite rules: \begin{verbatim} | tran {s1 s2 s3 : SortGeneratedTopCell} (t1 : Rewrites s1 s2) (t2 : Rewrites s2 s3) : Rewrites s1 s3 \end{verbatim}
nodes.statement_short: Inductive relation on KEVM states whose constructors are the extracted (summary) rewrite rules, with requires-clauses as arguments and a transitivity constructor.
nodes.label: def:Rewrites

nodes.name: X_bad_pc
nodes.statement: Given \begin{itemize} \item a single-opcode program $P$, \item a gas amount greater than 1, \item the program counter set to 1, \item the symbolic and well constrained remaining inputs of $X$. \end{itemize} Executing $X$ on $P$ with a fully symbolic state with the above conditions is successful and returns an empty output with the following modifications to the symbolic state: \begin{itemize} \item The parameter \texttt{returnData} is empty. \item The \texttt{executionLength} is increased by one. \end{itemize}
assumptions: a single-opcode program $P$,
a gas amount greater than 1,
the program counter set to 1,
the symbolic and well constrained remaining inputs of $X$.
conclusions: Executing $X$ on $P$ with a fully symbolic state with the above conditions is successful and returns an empty output with the following modifications to the symbolic state:
nodes.statement_short: With pc=1 past a single-opcode program, X succeeds with empty output, empty returnData and executionLength+1.
nodes.label: thm:X_bad_pc

nodes.name: Proof of X_bad_pc
nodes.statement: Massaging with tactics the execution path that evaluates if the program counter is out of bounds derives this result.
nodes.statement_short: Symbolic execution with tactics of the out-of-bounds program-counter path.

nodes.name: _<_> schedule gas-constant function
nodes.statement: The \texttt{«_<_>_SCHEDULE_Int_ScheduleConst_Schedule»} function (or \texttt{_<_>} for short) takes as arguments a gas constant (such as $G_{\text{verylow}}$) and a schedule (such as CANCUN) and returns how much is that gas constant in that schedule.
nodes.statement_short: Function returning the value of a gas constant in a given schedule (hardfork).
nodes.label: def:gasConstSched

nodes.name: _<<_>> schedule flag function
nodes.statement: The function \texttt{«_<<_>>_SCHEDULE_Bool_ScheduleFlag_Schedule»} (or \texttt{_<<_>>} for short) takes as arguments a schedule flag (such as $G_{\text{hascreate2}}$) and a schedule and returns the corresponding boolean if the schedule has the schedule flag. This is used to discriminate which rules can be applied depending on the schedule we're working with. In this example, working on an schedule \texttt{SCHED}, any rule involving the \texttt{CREATE2} opcode will have to satisfy $G_{\text{hascreate2}}$\texttt{<< SCHED >>} in order to be applied.
nodes.statement_short: Function returning whether a schedule has a given flag; used to gate rules by hardfork.
nodes.label: def:flagConstSched

conclusions: we equate \texttt{«_<_>_SCHEDULE_Int_ScheduleConst_Schedule» const .CANCUN_EVM} to a simple match statement on \texttt{const}.
nodes.statement_short: The gas-constant function at the Cancun schedule equals a simple match on the constant.

nodes.name: stateMap
nodes.statement: KEVM states are represented by the type \href{https://runtimeverification.github.io/evm-equivalence/docs/EvmEquivalence/KEVM2Lean/Sorts.html#SortGeneratedTopCell}{\texttt{SortGeneratedTopCell}}. Hence, we will be taking as input a \texttt{SortGeneratedTopCell} and converting it to an \href{https://runtimeverification.github.io/evm-equivalence/docs/EvmYul/EVM/State.html#EvmYul.EVM.State}{\texttt{EVM.State}}. The state mapping function will take an extra \texttt{EVM.State} argument to perform the identity mapping on the parts of the state that are not yet mapped.
nodes.statement_short: Maps a KEVM state (SortGeneratedTopCell) to an EVM.State, using an extra EVM.State for unmapped parts.
nodes.label: def:stateMap

nodes.name: Axiomatic cell-map functions
nodes.statement: To this effect, we postulate as axioms the existence of the \href{https://runtimeverification.github.io/evm-equivalence/docs/EvmEquivalence/Interfaces/Axioms.html}{following functions}: \begin{itemize} \item \texttt{SortAccountsCellMap}: maps \texttt{SortAccoutsCell} to \texttt{AccountMap}. \item \texttt{SortAccessedStorageCellMap}: maps \texttt{SortAccessedStorageCell} to the type of \texttt{accessedStorageKeys}. \item \texttt{SortStorageCellMap}: maps \texttt{SortStorageCell} to \texttt{Storage}. \item \texttt{SortTransientStorageCellMap}: maps \texttt{SortTransientStorageCell} to \texttt{Storage}. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Axiomatically postulated maps from KEVM account/storage cells to EvmYul maps.

nodes.name: Behavioral axioms for cell maps
nodes.statement: Since these are uninterpreted functions, we also assert \href{https://runtimeverification.github.io/evm-equivalence/docs/EvmEquivalence/StateMap.html#Axioms.findAccountInAccountCellMap}{behavioral axioms} on how these functions have to behave. These axioms serve as a blueprint for any future implementation of these functions, since whatever implementation is chosen should render the behavioral axioms as theorems.
nodes.statement_short: Behavioral axioms constrain the uninterpreted cell-map functions, as blueprints for future implementations.

nodes.name: EVM.step
nodes.statement: \texttt{EVM.step} orchestrates opcode execution, taking the following arguments. \begin{itemize} \item Amount of gas left: \texttt{fuel} \item Cost of executing the opcode: \texttt{gasCost} \item Opcode to be executed: \texttt{instr} \end{itemize} Given these arguments and an \texttt{EVM.state}, the \texttt{step} function will perform the correspondent updates on the provided state according to the semantics of \texttt{instr}.
nodes.statement_short: EvmYul function executing one opcode on a state given fuel, gas cost and an optional instruction.
nodes.label: def:EVM.step

nodes.name: Remarks on EVM.step arguments
nodes.statement: From this definition there are a couple of things to be noted. \begin{itemize} \item The \texttt{instr} parameter is of type \texttt{Option} and as such can be \texttt{none}, in which case the opcode is fetched from the execution environment's bytecode. \item \texttt{gasCost} is always given by functions calling \texttt{step}. \item If \texttt{fuel} is not strictly positive, \texttt{step} will immediately fail. \end{itemize} This means that while the \texttt{step} function captures a big portion of the executed opcode's semantics, it is not the full picture.
nodes.statement_short: instr may be none (fetched from bytecode), gasCost comes from callers, nonpositive fuel fails; so step is not the full semantics.

nodes.name: EVM.X
nodes.statement: Formalization of the yellow paper's $X$ function as defined in section 9.4. Given the following arguments: \begin{itemize} \item Amount of gas left: \texttt{fuel}. \item Valid jumpdests: \texttt{validJumps}. \item An \texttt{EVM.State}: \texttt{evmState}. \end{itemize} The function \texttt{X} performs the following tasks: \begin{itemize} \item Decode the opcodes present in \texttt{evmState}'s execution environment. \item Perform sanity checks and halt execution if these are not met. \item Assign gas costs depending on the decoded opcode. \item Execute \texttt{EVM.step} with the current decoded opcode. \item Iterate if the conditions are right. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Yellow-paper X function: decodes opcodes, checks, assigns gas, runs EVM.step and iterates.
nodes.label: def:EVM.X

nodes.name: summarization theorems
nodes.statement: Given a fully symbolic \texttt{EVM.State} $S$, summarization theorems clearly state which are the precise state updates that occur to $S$ after executing the \texttt{step} or \texttt{X} functions with the following: \begin{itemize} \item A set of concrete opcodes. \item Enough gas to perform execution. \item Well-formedness of other inputs to the functions such as a symbolic stack. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Summarization theorems give the exact state updates of step/X on a symbolic state for a set of opcodes, enough gas and well-formed inputs.

nodes.name: KEVM–EvmYul bisimulation
nodes.statement: The overarching goal is to prove that there exists a bisimulation relation between KEVM and the EvmYul model.

nodes.name: Bisimulation relation
nodes.statement: Given a transition system $(S, \rightarrow)$, a binary relation $R$ on $S$ is a bisimulation if and only if for every pair of states $(p, q)\in R$ we have: \begin{itemize} \item if $p \rightarrow p'$ then there is $q \rightarrow q'$ with $(p', q') \in R$; \item if $q \rightarrow q'$ then there is $p \rightarrow p'$ with $(p', q') \in R$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: R is a bisimulation if every transition of one related state is matched by a transition of the other into related states.
nodes.label: def:bisimulation

nodes.name: State space S, relation R and stateMap'
nodes.statement: In our context, \begin{itemize} \item $S$ is the union of both KEVM and EvmYul states ($S_{\text{KEVM}}$ and $S_{\text{EvmYul}}$ respectively). So we have $S_{\text{KEVM}}\, \bigcup\, S_{\text{EvmYul}} = S$ and $S_{\text{KEVM}}\, \bigcap\, S_{\text{EvmYul}} = \emptyset$. \item The transition relation $\rightarrow$ is execution in any of the models. In particular, we have that $\rightarrow\, \subset S_{\text{KEVM}} \times S_{\text{KEVM}} \,\bigcup\, S_{\text{EvmYul}} \times S_{\text{EvmYul}}$. \item $R = \bigl\{\bigl( p, \text{stateMap}(p) \bigr)\, |\, p\in S_{\text{KEVM}}\bigr\} \,\bigcup\, \bigl\{\bigl(\text{stateMap}'(q), q\bigr)\, |\, q\in S_{\text{EvmYul}}\bigr\}$ where $\text{stateMap}$ is defined in \ref{def:stateMap} and $\text{stateMap}'\,:\, S_{\text{EvmYul}}\rightarrow S_{\text{KEVM}}$ has not yet been defined. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: S is the disjoint union of KEVM and EvmYul states; R pairs each KEVM state with its stateMap image (and the inverse map).

nodes.name: Reduction of the first bisimulation implication
nodes.statement: Given KEVM states $p, p'$ with $p \rightarrow p'$, we know that $\bigl( p, \text{stateMap}(p) \bigr)$ and $\bigl( p', \text{stateMap}(p') \bigr)$ belong to $R$. Hence, to prove the first item we only need to show that $\text{stateMap}(p) \rightarrow \text{stateMap}(p')$.
nodes.statement_short: The first bisimulation clause reduces to showing stateMap(p) -> stateMap(p') whenever p -> p' in KEVM.

nodes.name: Transition function
nodes.statement: Given $p, p' \in S$, we have that $p\rightarrow p'$ if \begin{itemize} \item $p, p'\in S_{\text{KEVM}}$ and \texttt{Rewrites} $p$ $p'$ holds. \item $p, p'\in S_{\text{EvmYul}}$ and executing the \texttt{step}[\ref{def:EVM.step}] or \texttt{X}[\ref{def:EVM.X}] function on $p$ yields $p'$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: p -> p' iff Rewrites p p' (KEVM) or step/X maps p to p' (EvmYul).

nodes.name: First bisimulation implication (KEVM to EvmYul)
nodes.statement: \forall p, p'\in S_{\text{KEVM}}\,\, \texttt{Rewrites}\,\, p \,\, p' \Rightarrow f\bigl(\text{stateMap}(p)\bigr) = \text{stateMap}(p').
nodes.statement_short: Every KEVM rewrite p to p' is matched: f(stateMap p) = stateMap p'.
nodes.label: eq:bisimulation-explicit1

nodes.name: Second bisimulation implication (EvmYul to KEVM)
nodes.statement: \forall q, q'\in S_{\text{EvmYul}}\,\, f(q) = q' \Rightarrow \texttt{Rewrites}\,\, \text{stateMap}'(q)\,\, \text{stateMap}'(q').
nodes.statement_short: Every EvmYul execution q to q' is matched by a KEVM rewrite between stateMap' images.
nodes.label: eq:bisimulation-explicit2

nodes.name: stackOps_op opcode class
nodes.statement: Class of opcodes consisting of \texttt{DIV}, \texttt{SDIV}, \texttt{MOD}, \texttt{SMOD}, \texttt{SIGNEXT}, \texttt{SLT}, \texttt{SGT}, \texttt{AND}, \texttt{XOR}, \texttt{NOT}, \texttt{BYTE}, \texttt{SHL}, \texttt{SHR}, \texttt{SAR}.
nodes.statement_short: Opcode class DIV, SDIV, MOD, SMOD, SIGNEXT, SLT, SGT, AND, XOR, NOT, BYTE, SHL, SHR, SAR.
nodes.label: def:OneOp.stackOps

nodes.name: Rewrites restricted to stackOps_op
nodes.statement: The first stop is to, given the class of opcodes \texttt{stackOps_op}, identify all $p, p'\in S_{\text{KEVM}}$ such that $\texttt{Rewrites}\,\, p \,\, p'$ holds by means of executing any of the opcodes in that equivalence class (written as $\texttt{Rewrites}_{\texttt{stackOps_op}}\,\, p \,\, p'$).

nodes.name: oneOpLHS
nodes.statement: \texttt{oneOpLHS} is a symbolic state representing all KEVM states that rewrite to some other state by means of executing any opcode from the \texttt{stackOps_op} class. Viewed as a function, $$\mathcal{Im}(\texttt{oneOpLHS}) \supset \{p\,\, |\,\, \exists p'\,\,\texttt{Rewrites}_{\texttt{stackOps_op}}\,\, p \,\, p'\}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Symbolic KEVM state covering all states that rewrite via a stackOps_op opcode.
nodes.label: def:oneOpLHS

nodes.name: oneOpRHS
nodes.statement: \texttt{oneOpRHS} is a symbolic state representing all KEVM states that are a rewrite of some other state by means of executing any opcode from the \texttt{stackOps_op} class. Viewed as a function, $$\mathcal{Im}(\texttt{oneOpRHS}) \supset \{p'\,\, |\,\, \exists p\,\,\texttt{Rewrites}_{\texttt{stackOps_op}}\,\, p \,\, p'\}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Symbolic KEVM state covering all states reached by a stackOps_op rewrite.
nodes.label: def:oneOpRHS

nodes.name: Unrestricted Rewrites oneOpLHS oneOpRHS is false
nodes.statement: Note that, \texttt{oneOpLHS} and \texttt{oneOpRHS} being symbolic states, it is also correct to state \texttt{Rewrites} \texttt{oneOpLHS} \texttt{oneOpRHS}. However, this means that \texttt{oneOpLHS} rewrites to \texttt{oneOpRHS} for all possible value of its symbolic parameters. This is generally a false statement without restricting their symbolic values.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrites oneOpLHS oneOpRHS for all symbolic parameter values is generally false without restrictions.

nodes.name: Rewrites oneOpLHS oneOpRHS
nodes.statement: Given the restrictions posed by the \texttt{Rewrites} constructors corresponding to the \texttt{stackOps_op} opcode class, $\texttt{Rewrites}_{\texttt{stackOps_op}}$ \texttt{oneOpLHS} \texttt{oneOpRHS}.
assumptions: Given the restrictions posed by the \texttt{Rewrites} constructors corresponding to the \texttt{stackOps_op} opcode class
nodes.statement_short: Under the stackOps_op constructor conditions, oneOpLHS rewrites to oneOpRHS.
nodes.label: thm:oneOpRw

nodes.name: Proof of Rewrites oneOpLHS oneOpRHS
nodes.statement: We have that \texttt{oneOpLHS} and \texttt{oneOpRHS} are generalizations of the states represented in the \texttt{Rewrites} constructors for the \texttt{stackOps_op} class. As such, if we specialize the definitions of \texttt{oneOpLHS} and \texttt{oneOpRHS} down to the opcode, since we're assuming the conditions of satisfaction for every \texttt{stackOps_op} opcode summary, the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Specialize the symbolic states to each opcode and use the assumed summary conditions.

nodes.name: oneOpLHS_equiv
nodes.statement: This theorem allows for a clean rewrite of $\text{stateMap}(\texttt{oneOpLHS})$.
nodes.statement_short: Clean rewrite of stateMap(oneOpLHS).
nodes.label: thm:oneOpLHS_equiv

nodes.name: Proof of oneOpLHS_equiv
nodes.statement: This result follows by specifying it down to the opcode and executing the stateMap function.
nodes.statement_short: Specialize to the opcode and evaluate stateMap.

nodes.name: oneOpRHS_equiv
nodes.statement: This theorem allows for a clean rewrite of $\text{stateMap}(\texttt{oneOpRHS})$. We typically go beyond just a pure rewrite of the stateMap function and also simplify some of the initial expressions present either in \texttt{oneOpRHS} or as a result of the stateMap computation.
nodes.statement_short: Clean (simplified) rewrite of stateMap(oneOpRHS).
nodes.label: thm:oneOpRHS_equiv

nodes.name: Proof of oneOpRHS_equiv
nodes.statement: This result follows by specifying it down to the opcode and executing the stateMap function.
nodes.statement_short: Specialize to the opcode and evaluate stateMap.

nodes.name: step_oneOp
nodes.statement: Assume \begin{itemize} \item All the conditions needed to satisfy the summaries of $\texttt{Rewrites}_{\texttt{stackOps_op}}$, \item A schedule set to CANCUN, \item Enough gas per opcode, \item Well formed gas and program counter parameters in \texttt{oneOpLHS}, \item Non-negative elements in the stack of \texttt{oneOpLHS}. \end{itemize} Then, evaluating the function \texttt{EVM.step} with any of the \texttt{stackOps_op} opcodes on $\text{stateMap}(\texttt{oneOpLHS})$ results in $\text{stateMap}(\texttt{oneOpRHS})$.
assumptions: All the conditions needed to satisfy the summaries of $\texttt{Rewrites}_{\texttt{stackOps_op}}$,
A schedule set to CANCUN,
Enough gas per opcode,
Well formed gas and program counter parameters in \texttt{oneOpLHS},
Non-negative elements in the stack of \texttt{oneOpLHS}.
conclusions: evaluating the function \texttt{EVM.step} with any of the \texttt{stackOps_op} opcodes on $\text{stateMap}(\texttt{oneOpLHS})$ results in $\text{stateMap}(\texttt{oneOpRHS})$.
nodes.statement_short: Under summary conditions, Cancun, enough gas and well-formedness, EVM.step on stateMap(oneOpLHS) gives stateMap(oneOpRHS).
nodes.label: thm:step_oneOp

nodes.name: Proof of step_oneOp
nodes.statement: The proof consists of several parts, but many are shared among the \texttt{stackOps_op} class, such as the gas or program counter proof obligations. The main semantic challenge for this class of opcodes is to show that the operations performed on the stack correspond to each other. So, for example, for the \texttt{DIV} case, once all the execution-related bureaucracies have been dealt with, the main goal is the following: \begin{verbatim} intMap W0 / intMap W1 = intMap (divWord W0 W1) \end{verbatim} Where \texttt{W0} and \texttt{W1} are the first two elements of \texttt{oneOpLHS}'s stack. What this proof obligation is stating is that mapping the first two elements of a KEVM stack to EvmYul and then dividing them, is the same as dividing the two elements in KEVM and them mapping them to EvmYul.
nodes.statement_short: Discharge shared gas/pc obligations, then show stack operations commute with intMap. E.g. for DIV: intMap W0 / intMap W1 = intMap (divWord W0 W1).

nodes.name: X_oneOp
nodes.statement: Assume \begin{itemize} \item All the conditions needed to satisfy the summaries of $\texttt{Rewrites}_{\texttt{stackOps_op}}$, \item A schedule set to CANCUN, \item Enough gas per opcode, \item Well formed gas parameter in \texttt{oneOpLHS}, \item The program counter of \texttt{oneOpLHS} set to zero, \item Non-negative elements in the stack of \texttt{oneOpLHS}, \item A well formed stack in \texttt{oneOpLHS} \item The program to be executed in \texttt{oneOpLHS} be a single-opcode program consisting of any opcode of the \texttt{stackOps_op} class. \end{itemize} Then, evaluating the function \texttt{EVM.X} with any of the \texttt{stackOps_op} opcodes on $\text{stateMap}(\texttt{oneOpLHS})$ results in $\text{stateMap}(\texttt{oneOpRHS})$.
assumptions: All the conditions needed to satisfy the summaries of $\texttt{Rewrites}_{\texttt{stackOps_op}}$,
A schedule set to CANCUN,
Enough gas per opcode,
Well formed gas parameter in \texttt{oneOpLHS},
The program counter of \texttt{oneOpLHS} set to zero,
Non-negative elements in the stack of \texttt{oneOpLHS},
A well formed stack in \texttt{oneOpLHS}
The program to be executed in \texttt{oneOpLHS} be a single-opcode program consisting of any opcode of the \texttt{stackOps_op} class.
conclusions: evaluating the function \texttt{EVM.X} with any of the \texttt{stackOps_op} opcodes on $\text{stateMap}(\texttt{oneOpLHS})$ results in $\text{stateMap}(\texttt{oneOpRHS})$.
nodes.statement_short: Under summary conditions and well-formedness for a single-opcode program, EVM.X on stateMap(oneOpLHS) gives stateMap(oneOpRHS).
nodes.label: thm:X_oneOp

nodes.name: Proof of X_oneOp
nodes.statement: Similarly as for the \texttt{EVM.step} function, we use tactics to execute \texttt{EVM.X} symbolically. The hypothesis space allows us to get rid of all reverting cases and confront the semantic equivalence similarly as in the proof for the \texttt{EVM.step} function.
nodes.statement_short: Symbolic execution of EVM.X with tactics; hypotheses remove reverting cases, then reuse the step argument.

nodes.name: Simulation for stackOps_op opcodes
nodes.statement: With these two theorems proven we can conclude that under the conditions of satisfaction of the summaries for the \texttt{stackOps_op} opcodes, together with some well-formedness constraints, there is a similarity relationship (equation \ref{eq:bisimulation-explicit1}) between executing the \texttt{stackOps_op} opcodes in KEVM and executing them in the EvmYul model.
assumptions: under the conditions of satisfaction of the summaries for the \texttt{stackOps_op} opcodes, together with some well-formedness constraints
conclusions: there is a similarity relationship (equation \ref{eq:bisimulation-explicit1}) between executing the \texttt{stackOps_op} opcodes in KEVM and executing them in the EvmYul model.
nodes.statement_short: Equation (1) (KEVM-to-EvmYul simulation) holds for the stackOps_op opcodes under summary and well-formedness conditions.

nodes.statement_short: Most gas/pc obligations are shared across the class.

nodes.name: Reduce DIV case to intMap commutation
nodes.statement: The main semantic challenge for this class of opcodes is to show that the operations performed on the stack correspond to each other. So, for example, for the \texttt{DIV} case, once all the execution-related bureaucracies have been dealt with, the main goal is the following: \begin{verbatim} intMap W0 / intMap W1 = intMap (divWord W0 W1) \end{verbatim} Where \texttt{W0} and \texttt{W1} are the first two elements of \texttt{oneOpLHS}'s stack.
nodes.statement_short: Main goal: stack operation commutes with intMap, e.g. DIV.

nodes.name: Interpret the obligation
nodes.statement: What this proof obligation is stating is that mapping the first two elements of a KEVM stack to EvmYul and then dividing them, is the same as dividing the two elements in KEVM and them mapping them to EvmYul.
nodes.statement_short: The obligation says map-then-divide equals divide-then-map.

nodes.name: Unproven SortK DecidableEq/LawfulBEq instances
nodes.statement: There are two instances that we have declared without providing any proof due to time constraints. For the \texttt{SortK} we have declared instances of the \texttt{DecidableEq} and \texttt{LawfulBEq} classes without providing any proofs.

nodes.name: Correctness of the K framework
nodes.statement: \textbf{K framework:} Correct implementation of Matching Logic, of which a deep embbedding already exists formalized in Lean 4.

nodes.name: Correctness of KEVM summarization
nodes.statement: \textbf{KEVM summarization:} The summarization tooling built in KEVM that produces the ``compressed'' rewrite rules containing the computational content of the opcodes is correctly done.

nodes.name: Faithfulness of K-to-Lean extraction
nodes.statement: \textbf{K-to-Lean extraction:} The \texttt{klean} tool built into K does a faithful enough conversion of the compiled Kore theory from the evm-semantics.

nodes.name: Well-formedness constraints
nodes.statement: \textbf{Well-formedness constraints:} Due to how the summaries are generated, some of the symbolic parameters are under-constrained. For instance, KEVM words are unbouned integers. The semantics implements checks that ensure these symbolic parameters are indeed within the correct ranges. However, since the summaries extract the computational behavior after the appropriate checks are performed, we have to add these as extra hypotheses. Other necessary hypotheses are also added such as there being enough gas to execute the opcode.
nodes.statement_short: Extra hypotheses bound under-constrained symbolic parameters (e.g. words in range) and ensure enough gas.

nodes.name: Reliance on unproven results
nodes.statement: \textbf{Unproven results:} There is a number of unproven results in which we rely. These range from axioms (which most should be turned into theorems and proven) and theorems with no proofs or missing subgoals.

nodes.name: Opcode-level bisimilarity implies program-level bisimilarity
nodes.statement: We believe showing bisimilarity at the opcode level should guarantee bisimilarity when executing full EVM programs.
assumptions: showing bisimilarity at the opcode level
conclusions: should guarantee bisimilarity when executing full EVM programs
